Two particles A and B of masses m and km respectively are placed on a smooth horizontal plane. Particle A is made to move on the plane with speed u so as to collide directly with B, which is at rest. After the collision B moves with speed \(\frac{3}{10} u\).\par \textbf{a)} Find, in terms of u and the constant k, the speed of A after the collision.\par [4 marks]\par \textbf{b)} By using Newton's law of restitution, show that \(\frac{7}{3}\leq k\leq \frac{17}{3}\)\par [5 marks]\par Problem-solving\par In part b use the limits of e to set up an inequality.

Before collision After collision\par \(\overrightarrow{u}\) At rest \(\bigcirc\)\par \(B(km)\)\par \(\overrightarrow{v}\)\par \(\bigcirc\)\par \(0.3u\)\par \(\bigcirc\)\par \(B(km)\)\par Using conservation of linear momentum for the system \((\rightarrow)\): [M1]\par \(mu=mv+km0.3u\) [M1] [A1]
\(\Rightarrow v=u(1-0.3k)\) (cancelling out the common factor m) [A1]

\textbf{b)} Using Newton's law of restitution:\par \(\frac{0.3 u-v}{u-0}=e\) [M1]\par So using the result from part a\par \(0.3 u-u(1-0.3 k)=e u\) [A1]\par \(\Rightarrow e=0.3 k-0.7\) [A1]\par As \(0\leqslant e\leqslant 1\), therefore \(0\leqslant 0.3 k-0.7\leqslant 1\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow 0.7\leqslant 0.3 k\leqslant 1.7\)\par \(\Rightarrow \frac{7}{3}\leqslant k\leqslant \frac{17}{3}\) [A1]

transcription.tex: Question 9

Two particles A and B of masses m and 3m respectively are placed on a smooth horizontal plane. Particle A is made to move on the plane with speed 2u so as to collide directly with B which is moving in the same direction with speed u. After the collision B moves with speed ku where k is a constant.\par \textbf{a)} Find, in terms of u and the constant k, the speed of A after the collision. [4 marks]\par \textbf{b)} By using Newton's law of restitution, show that \(\frac{5}{4}\leq k\leq \frac{3}{2}\) [5 marks]

Using conservation of linear momentum for the system \((\rightarrow)\): [M1]\par \(2mu+3mu=vm+3kmu\) [M1] [A1]\par \(\Rightarrow v=u(5-3k)\) (cancelling out the common factor m) [A1]\par \textbf{b)} Using Newton's law of restitution:\par \(\frac{ku-v}{2u-u}=e\) [M1]\par So using the result from part a\par \(ku-u(5-3k)=eu\) [A1]\par \(\Rightarrow e=4k-5\) [A1]
As \(0\leqslant e\leqslant 1\), therefore \(0\leqslant 4k-5\leqslant 1\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow 5\leqslant 4k\leqslant 6\)
\(\Rightarrow \frac{5}{4}\leqslant k\leqslant \frac{3}{2}\) [A1]

transcription.tex: Question 10

A particle P of mass m is moving with speed 4u on a smooth horizontal plane. The particle collides directly with a particle Q of mass 3m moving with speed 2u in the same direction as P. The coefficient of restitution between P and Q is e.\par \textbf{a)} Show that the speed of Q after the collision is \(\frac{u}{2} ( 5+e).\) [6 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Find the speed of P after the collision, giving your answer in terms of e. [4 marks]\par \textbf{c)} Show that the direction of motion of P is unchanged by the collision. [2 marks]\par \textbf{d)} Given that the magnitude of the impulse of P on Q is 2mu, find the value of e. [4 marks]

Using conservation of linear momentum for the system \((\rightarrow)\):\par \(m \times 4u + 3m \times 2u = mv_1 + 3mv_2\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow 3v_2 + v_1 = 10u\) [A1]\par (cancelling out the common factor \(m\)) (1)\par Using Newton's law of restitution:\par \(e = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{4u - 2u} = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{2u}\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow v_2 - v_1 = 2ue\) (2) [A1]\par Adding equations (1) and (2) gives:
\textbf{b)} Substituting into equation (1) gives: [M1]

\(\frac{3u}{2}(5 + e) + v_1 = 10u\) [A1]\par \(2v_1 = 20u - 15u - 3ue\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow v_1 = \frac{u}{2}(5 - 3e)\) [A1]\par \textbf{c)} The direction of motion of \(P\) is unchanged provided that \(\frac{u}{2}(5 - 3e) > 0\), i.e. \(e < \frac{5}{3}\) [M1]\par This must be the case as \(0 \leqslant e \leqslant 1\) [A1]\par \textbf{d)} Change of momentum of \(Q = 3m(v_2 - 2u)\) [M1]\par \(= 3m\left(\frac{5u}{2} + \frac{eu}{2} - 2u\right)\)\par \(= \frac{3mu}{2}(1 + e)\) [A1]\par As impulse of \(P =\) change in momentum of \(Q\), this gives:\par \(2mu = \frac{3mu}{2}(1 + e)\) [M1]
\(\Rightarrow e = \frac{1}{3}\) [A1]

A particle of mass m kg lies on a smooth horizontal surface. Initially the particle is at rest at a point O midway between a pair of fixed parallel vertical walls. The walls are 2 m apart. At time t=0 the particle is projected from O with speed u m \(s^{-1}\) in a direction perpendicular to the walls. The coefficient of restitution between the particle and each wall is \(\frac{2}{3}\). The magnitude of the impulse on the particle due to the first impact with a wall is \(\lambda m u\) N s.\par (a) Find the value of \(\lambda\).\par [3 marks]\par The particle returns to O, having bounced off each wall once, at time t=3 seconds.\par (b) Find the value of u.\par [6 marks]
Speed after impact \(=\tfrac23u\)\par Impulse = change in momentum \(=\pm(m\cdot\tfrac23u-m\cdot(-u))=\tfrac53mu\)\par \(\lambda=\tfrac53\)
Question 6

A particle falls 3 m from rest onto a smooth horizontal plane. It then rebounds to a height h m. The coefficient of restitution between the particle and the plane is 0.25.\par \textbf{a)} Find the value of h. [4 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Without further calculation, state how your answer to part a would change if \(e>0.25\) [1 mark]

\textbf{a)} The particle falls under gravity. Find the speed of the particle when it hits the plane by using the constant acceleration formula \(v^{2}=u^{2}+2as\), where s=3, a=g and u=0. This gives:\par \(v^{2}=2\times g\times 3=6g\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{6g}\)\par It hits the ground and rebounds. Use Newton's law of restitution to find the speed of rebound:\par \(e=0.25=\frac{\mathrm{speed of rebound}}{\mathrm{speed of approach}}=\frac{\mathrm{speed of rebound}}{\sqrt{6g}}\)\par \(\Rightarrow \mathrm{speed of rebound}=0.25\sqrt{6g}\) [M1]

It rebounds and moves under gravity. Find the height the particle rebounds to by using the constant acceleration formula \(v^{2}=u^{2}+2as\), where s=h, a=-g, u=0.25 \(\sqrt{6g}\) and v=0. This gives:\par \(0=\left(0.25\sqrt{6g}\right)^{2}-2gh\) [M1]

\(2gh=0.0625\times 6g\)\par \(\Rightarrow h=\frac{0.375g}{2g}=0.1875\)\par So the particle rebounds to a height of 18.75 cm. [A1]\par \textbf{b)} If e>0.25 the collision between the sphere and the plane would be more elastic, so the particle would rebound to a greater height. [B1]
Question 7

A small smooth sphere falls from rest onto a smooth horizontal plane and rebounds from the plane. It takes 2 seconds to reach the plane then another 2 seconds to reach the plane a second time. Find the coefficient of restitution between the sphere and the plane. [7 marks]

The sphere falls under gravity. Find the speed of the particle when it hits the plane by using the constant acceleration formula \(v=u+at\) [M1], where \(t=2\), \(a=g=9.8\) and \(u=0\). This gives: \(v=u+at \Rightarrow v=2g\) [A1]\par The sphere then bounces and its speed of rebound is \(2ge\) [M1], where e is the coefficient of restitution. It then moves under gravity for 2 seconds. Find e, by considering the motion after the first impact using the constant acceleration formula \(s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}\), where \(s=0\), \(t=2\), \(a=-g=-9.8\) and \(u=2ge\) [A1]\par This gives: \(0=2ge\times 2-\frac{g}{2}\times 4=4ge-2g\) [M1]\par Rearranging gives \(4ge=2g\), so \(e=2g/(4g)=1/2\). [M1]
The coefficient of restitution is \(\frac{1}{2}\) [A1]
Question 8

A small smooth sphere falls from rest onto a smooth horizontal plane. It takes 3 seconds to reach the plane. The coefficient of restitution between the sphere and the plane is 0.49. Find the time it takes after rebound for the sphere to reach the plane a second time. [7 marks]

The sphere falls under gravity. Find the speed of the particle when it hits the plane by using the constant acceleration formula \(v=u+at\) [M1], where \(t=3\), \(a=g=9.8\) and \(u=0\). This gives: \(v=u+at=3g\) [A1]\par The sphere then bounces and its speed of rebound is \(3ge\) [M1], where e is the coefficient of restitution, i.e. speed of rebound \(=3\times0.49g=1.47g\). It then moves under gravity for t seconds before bouncing a second time. Find t, by considering the motion after the first impact using the constant acceleration formula \(s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}\) [A1], where \(s=0\), \(a=-g=-9.8\) and \(u=1.47g\) [M1]. This gives:\par \(0=1.47gt-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2}\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow t=\frac{2\times1.47g}{g}=2.94\) s [A1]
Question 9

A particle falls from rest from a height of h m above level ground. After rebounding the particle reaches a maximum height of \(\frac{1}{2} h\). Find, in terms of g and h, the height of the particle 1 second after it hits the ground. [8 marks]

After it rebounds the particle moves under gravity to a height of 0.5h m. Find the speed of the particle when it rebounds from the plane by using the constant acceleration formula \(v^{2}=u^{2}+2as\), where \(s=0.5h\), \(a=-g\) and \(v=0\). This gives: [M1]\par \(0=u^{2}-2g\times 0.5h\) [M1]\par \(u^{2}=gh\)\par \(\Rightarrow u=\sqrt{gh}\) [A1]\par Find the height of the particle 1 second after it rebounds from the plane by using the constant acceleration formula \(s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}\) [M1], where \(t=1\) [M1], \(a=-g=-9.8\) [A1] and \(u=\sqrt{gh}\) [A1]. This gives:\par \(s=\left\{\sqrt{gh}-\frac{g}{2}\right\}\) [A1]

transcription.tex: Question 8

A truck of mass 5 tonnes is moving in a straight line at \(1.5\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) towards a second stationary truck of mass 10 tonnes which is at rest. The trucks collide, and after the impact the second truck moves at \(0.6\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Modelling the trucks as particles, find:\par \textbf{a)} the velocity of the first truck after the impact [3 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the coefficient of restitution between the two trucks [2 marks]\par \textbf{c)} the loss of kinetic energy due to the impact. [3 marks]\par Hint  1 tonne = 1000 kg

(a) Take the initial direction of truck A as positive. Conservation of momentum gives \(5000(1.5)+10000(0)=5000v+10000(0.6)\). [M1] [A1]\par \(50v=75-60=15\), so \(v=0.3\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) forwards. [A1]\par (b) The speed of separation is \(0.6-0.3\) [M1]; the speed of approach is \(1.5-0\). Thus \(e=(0.6-0.3)/1.5=1/5=0.2\) [A1].

\textbf{c)} The energy lost is \(E_{\rm initial}-E_{\rm final}\) [M1]. Substitute the two masses and their speeds: \(\frac12(5000)(1.5)^2-\left[\frac12(5000)(0.3)^2+\frac12(10000)(0.6)^2\right]\) [A1]. The energy lost is \(5625-(225+1800)=3600\;\mathrm J\) [A1].
Question 10

A small smooth sphere A of mass 2 kg moves at \(4\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) on a smooth horizontal table. It collides directly with a second small smooth sphere B of mass 3 kg, which is moving in the same direction at a speed of \(1\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). The loss of kinetic energy due to the collision is 3 J. After the collision A and B continue to move in the same direction with speeds u and v respectively.\par \textbf{a)} Show that \(5 v^{2}-22 v+21=0\) [6 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Hence find u and v, carefully justifying your choice of solutions. [5 marks]

Using conservation of linear momentum for the system (\(\rightarrow\)):\par \(2 \times 4 + 3 \times 1 = 2u + 3v\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow 11 = 2u + 3v\) [A1]\par (1)\par Loss of kinetic energy \(= \text{initial kinetic energy} - \text{final kinetic energy}\)\par \(= \frac{1}{2} 2(4)^2 + \frac{1}{2} 3(1)^2 - \frac{1}{2} 2u^2 - \frac{1}{2} 3v^2\) [M1]\par \(= \frac{35}{2} - u^2 - \frac{3v^2}{2}\)
So as the loss of kinetic energy due to the collision is \(3\,\text{ J}\)\par \(\frac{35}{2} - u^2 - \frac{3v^2}{2} = 3\) [A1]

(2)\par From equation (1), \(2u = 11 - 3v\)\par So \((2u)^2 = (11 - 3v)^2\)\par \(4u^2 = (11 - 3v)^2\)\par Substituting into equation (2):\par \(58 = 6v^2 + (11 - 3v)^2\) [M1]\par \(58 = 6v^2 + 121 - 66v + 9v^2\)\par \(15v^2 - 66v + 63 = 0\)\par \(5v^2 - 22v + 21 = 0\) [A1]\par \textbf{b)} Using the quadratic formula to solve for \(v\)\par \(v = \frac{22 \pm \sqrt{22^2 - 4 \times 5 \times 21}}{10} = \frac{22 \pm \sqrt{22^2 - 4 \times 5 \times 21}}{10} = \frac{22 \pm \sqrt{64}}{10}\) [M1]\par \(v = \frac{22 \pm 8}{10} = 3 \text{ or } 1.4\) [A1]

Substituting into equation (1):\par \(v = 1.4 \Rightarrow 2u = 11 - (3 \times 1.4) = 6.8 \Rightarrow u = 3.4\) [M1]\par After the collision \(B\) must be moving faster than \(A\) as sphere \(A\) cannot pass through sphere \(B\), so reject this solution since \(v < u\) [A1]\par \(v = 3 \Rightarrow 2u = 11 - (3 \times 3) = 2 \Rightarrow u = 1\)\par This is a valid solution since \(v > u\), so \(v = 3 \text{ ms}^{-1}\) and \(u = 1 \text{ ms}^{-1}\). [A1]

Question 12

Two particles A and B, of masses m and M respectively, are connected by a light inextensible string. The particles are side by side on a smooth floor and A is projected with speed u directly away from B. When the string becomes taut, particle B is jerked into motion and A and B then move with a common speed in the direction of the original projection of A.\par Show that the loss of total kinetic energy due to the jerk is \(\frac{m M u^{2}}{2(m+M)}\) [8 marks]\par Problem-solving\par Start by finding an expression for the common speed, \(v\), after the string becomes taut.

Using conservation of linear momentum for the system \((\rightarrow)\): [M1]\par \(mu = Mv + mv\) [A1]\par \(\Rightarrow v = \frac{mu}{M + m}\) [A1]\par (1)\par Kinetic energy lost \(= \text{initial kinetic energy} - \text{final kinetic energy}\) [M1]\par \(= \frac{1}{2}mu^2 - \frac{1}{2}(M + m)v^2\) [A1]\par \(= \frac{1}{2}mu^2 - \frac{1}{2}(M + m)\frac{(mu)^2}{(M + m)^2}\) [M1]
Substituting for \(v\) from equation (1)\par \(= \frac{mu^2(M + m)}{2(M + m)} - \frac{m^2u^2}{2(M + m)}\)

Question 14

Three small spheres of masses 20 g, 40 g and 60 g respectively lie in order in a straight line on a large smooth table. The distance between adjacent spheres is 10 cm. Two slack strings, each 70 cm in length, connect the first sphere with the second, and the second sphere with the third. Find:\par \textbf{a)} the time which elapses before the 20 g sphere begins to move and the speed with which it starts [8 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the loss in kinetic energy resulting from the two jerks. [5 marks]

\(1.2w = 3\)\par \(\Rightarrow w = 2.5 \text{ms}^{-1}\) [A1]\par Until the first jerk, the \(60\text{g}\) sphere moves with speed \(5 \text{ms}^{-1}\) through \(0.6\,\text{m}\).\par So the time taken is \(\frac{0.6}{5} = 0.12\,\text{s}\) [M1] [A1]\par From the first jerk until the second jerk, the \(60\text{g}\) and \(40\text{g}\) spheres moves with speed \(3 \text{ms}^{-1}\) through \(0.6\,\text{m}\).\par So the time taken is \(\frac{0.6}{3} = 0.2\,\text{s}\) [M1]\par Therefore the time which elapses before the \(20\text{g}\) sphere begins to move is \(0.12 + 0.2 = 0.32\,\text{s}\) [A1]
\textbf{b)} The loss of kinetic energy \(= \text{initial kinetic energy} - \text{final kinetic energy}\) [M1]

Initially only one sphere moves, with \(E_i=\tfrac12(0.06)(5)^2=0.75\;\mathrm J\) [M1]. When all three move together, \(E_f=\tfrac12(0.06+0.04+0.02)(2.5)^2\) [M1], giving \(E_f=0.375\;\mathrm J\) [A1].\par \(= 0.75 - 0.375 = 0.375\,\text{ J}\) [A1]

The coefficient of restitution between each pair of particles is e. After the collision between P and Q there is a collision between Q and R.\par (a) Show that \(e > \frac{2}{3}\)\par [7 marks]\par It is given that \(e=\frac{3}{4}\)\par (b) Show that there will not be a further collision between P and Q.\par [6 marks]

transcription.tex: Question 4

Three identical spheres A, B and C of equal mass m move along the same straight line on a horizontal plane. A and B are moving in opposite directions towards each other with speeds 4u and 2u respectively. C is moving in the same direction as A with speed 3u.\par \textbf{a)} If the coefficient of restitution between any two of the spheres is e, show that B will only collide with C if \(e > \frac{2}{3}\) [8 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Find the direction of motion of A after collision, if \(e > \frac{2}{3}\) [2 marks]

Using conservation of linear momentum for the system \((\rightarrow)\):\par \(4u - 2u = v + w\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow v + w = 2u\) [A1]\par Using Newton's law of restitution:\par \(e = \frac{w - v}{4u + 2u}\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow w - v = 6eu\) [A1]\par Adding equations (1) and (2) gives:\par \(2w = 2u + 6ue\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow w = u(1 + 3e)\) [A1]
\(B\) will collide with \(C\) if the speed of \(B\) after collision with \(A\) is greater than the speed of \(C\), i.e. if \(w > 3u\). This will occur if:\par \(u(1 + 3e) > 3u\) [M1]

\(3e > 2 \Rightarrow e > \frac{2}{3}\) [A1]\par \textbf{b)} Subtracting equation (2) from equation (1) gives:\par \(2v = 2u - 6eu\)\par \(v = u(1 - 3e)\) [M1]\par If \(e > \frac{2}{3}\) then \(v < 0\), and the direction of \(A\) is reversed by the collision with \(B\). [A1]

transcription.tex: Question 5

Two particles P and Q of masses 2m and 3m respectively are moving in opposite directions on a smooth plane with speeds 4u and 2u respectively. The particles collide directly. The direction of motion of Q is reversed by the impact and its speed after impact is u. This particle then hits a smooth vertical wall perpendicular to its direction of motion. The coefficient of restitution between Q and the wall is \(\frac{2}{3}\). In the subsequent motion, there is a further collision between Q and P. Find the velocities of P and Q after this collision. [8 marks]

Using conservation of linear momentum for the system \((\rightarrow)\):\par \(2m \times 4u + 3m \times (-2u) = 2mv + 3mu\) [M1]\par \(2u = 2v + 3u \Rightarrow v = -0.5u\) [A1]\par Use this result to find the coefficient of restitution between particles \(P\) and \(Q\).\par \(e = \frac{u - v}{4u + 2u} = \frac{1.5u}{6u} = 0.25\) [M1]\par The second collision is between \(Q\) and the wall.
\(Q\) rebounds from the wall with velocity \(\frac{2}{3}u\), as the coefficient of restitution between \(Q\) and the wall is \(\frac{2}{3}\). [B1]
Using conservation of linear momentum for the system \((\leftarrow)\):\par \(2m \times \frac{1}{2}u + 3m \times \frac{2}{3}u = 2x + 3y\) [M1]

\(\Rightarrow 2x + 3y = 3u\) (1)\par Using Newton's law of restitution:\par \(e = \frac{1}{4} = \frac{x - y}{\frac{2}{3}u - \frac{1}{2}u}\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow x - y = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{6}u = \frac{u}{24}\) (2)\par Adding equation (1) to 3 \(\times\) equation (2) gives:\par \(5x = 3u + \frac{u}{8} = \frac{25u}{8} \Rightarrow x = \frac{5u}{8}\) [A1]\par Substituting into equation (2) gives:\par \(\frac{5u}{8} - y = \frac{u}{24} \Rightarrow y = \frac{15u - u}{24} = \frac{14u}{24} = \frac{7u}{12}\) [A1]

transcription.tex: Question 6

Two small smooth spheres P and Q have masses m and 3m respectively. Sphere P is moving with speed 12u on a smooth horizontal table when it collides directly with Q which is at rest on the table. The coefficient of restitution between P and Q is \(\frac{2}{3}\)\par \textbf{a)} Find the velocities of P and Q immediately after the collision. [6 marks]\par After the collision Q hits a smooth vertical wall perpendicular to the direction of its motion. The coefficient of restitution between Q and the wall is \(\frac{4}{5}\). Q then collides with P a second time.\par \textbf{b)} Find the velocities of P and Q after the second collision between P and Q. [8 marks]

Using conservation of linear momentum for the system (\(\rightarrow\)):\par \(m \times 12u = mv + 3mw\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow v + 3w = 12u\) [A1]\par Using Newton's law of restitution:\par \(e = \frac{2}{3} = \frac{w - v}{12u}\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow w - v = 8u\) [A1]\par Adding equation (1) to equation (2) gives:\par \(4w = 20u \Rightarrow w = 5u\) [A1]
Substituting into equation (2) gives:\par \(5u - v = 8u \Rightarrow v = -3u\)
After the collision the speed of \(P\) is \(3u\) and its direction is reversed, and the speed of \(Q\) is \(5u\). [A1]

\textbf{b)} \(Q\) then hits a wall and rebounds with speed \(\frac{4}{5} \times 5u = 4u\) [B1]\par Second collision between \(P\) and \(Q\)\par \(P(m) \quad Q(3m)\)\par After second collision\par \(P(m) \quad Q(3m)\)\par Using conservation of linear momentum for the system (\(\leftarrow\)):\par \(3mu + 12mu = mx + 3my \Rightarrow 3y + x = 15u\) [M1] [A1]\par Using Newton's law of restitution:\par \(e = \frac{2}{3} = \frac{x - y}{4u - 3u} \Rightarrow 3x - 3y = 2u\) [M1] [A1]\par Adding equation (1) to equation (2) gives:\par \(4x = 17u \Rightarrow x = \frac{17u}{4}\) [M1] [A1]
Substituting into equation (4) gives:\par \(\frac{51u}{4} - 3y = 2u \Rightarrow y = \frac{43u}{12}\) [A1]

transcription.tex: Question 7

A small table tennis ball, which may be modelled as a particle, falls from rest at a height 40 cm onto a smooth horizontal plane. The coefficient of restitution between the ball and the plane is 0.7.\par \textbf{a)} Find the height to which the ball rebounds after:\par i the first bounce\par ii the second bounce. [8 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Describe the subsequent motion of the ball. [1 mark]\par \textbf{c)} Find the total distance travelled by the ball before it comes to rest. [5 marks]\par Problem-solving\par Find the ratio between the heights of successive bounces according to the model.\par \textbf{d)} Give one reason why your answer to part c is unrealistic. [1 mark]

\textbf{a)} i Use \(v^{2}=u^{2}+2 a s\) downwards with \(u=0, s=0.4\) and \(a=g=9.8\) to find the speed of approach for the first bounce: [M1]\par \(v^{2}=2 g \times0.4=7.84\)\par \(v=2.8\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) [A1]\par Newton's law of restitution gives speed of rebound from floor as \(0.7 \times2.8=1.96\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) [M1]\par Use \(v^{2}=u^{2}+2 a s\) upwards with \(v=0, u=1.96\) and \(a=-g\) to find the height of the first bounce:\par \(0=1.96^{2}-2 g s\) [M1]\par \(s=\frac{1.96^{2}}{19.6}=0.196=19.6\) cm [A1]\par ii Use \(v^{2}=u^{2}+2 a s\) downwards with \(u=0, s=0.196\) and \(a=g=9.8\) to find the speed of approach for the second bounce:

\(v=1.96\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) [This result can also be directly deduced] [B1]\par Following second collision with floor, the ball rebounds with speed \(0.7 \times1.96=1.372\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) Use \(v^{2}=u^{2}+2 a s\) upwards with \(v=0, u=1.372\) and \(a=-g\) [M1]\par \(0=1.372^{2}-2 g s\)\par \(s=\frac{1.372^{2}}{19.6}=0.096 \ 04=9.604\) cm [A1]\par \textbf{b)} The ball continues to bounce (for an infinite amount of time) with its height decreasing by a common ratio each time. [B1]\par \textbf{c)} Ratio of heights of successive bounces is \(\frac{9.604}{19.6}=0.49\) [M1] Total distance travelled \(=0.4+(2 \times0.196+2 \times0.196 \times0.49+2 \times0.196 \times0.49 \times0.49 \dots)\) [A1]

The total distance after the first impact is a geometric series with first term \(a=2(0.196)\) [M1] and sum \(a/(1-r)\) [M1]. Including the original fall gives \(0.4+2(0.196)/(1-0.49)\) [A1].\par \(=1.17\,\mathrm{m}\) (3 s.f.)
\textbf{d)} The ball loses energy following every bounce, so an infinite number of bounces would be unrealistic. [B1]

transcription.tex: Question 8

A small smooth ball, which may be modelled as a particle, falls from rest at a height H onto a smooth horizontal plane. The coefficient of restitution between the ball and the plane is e.\par \textbf{a)} Find, in terms of H and e, the height to which the ball rebounds after the first bounce. [9 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Find, in terms of H and e, the height to which the ball rebounds after the second bounce.\par [6 marks]\par \textbf{c)} Find an expression for the total distance travelled by the ball before it comes to rest. [6 marks]\par Problem-solving\par Draw clear diagrams for each stage of the motion of the ball.

\textbf{a)} Use \(v^{2}=u^{2}+2as\) downwards with \(u=0, s=H\) and \(a=g\) [M1]\par \(v^{2}=2gH \Rightarrow v=\sqrt{2gH}\) [A1]\par Newton's law of restitution gives speed of separation from plane as \(e\sqrt{2gH}\) [M1] [A1]\par Let the height to which the ball rebounds after the first bounce be \(h_{1}\) [B1]\par Use \(v^{2}=u^{2}+2as\) upwards with \(v=0, u=e\sqrt{2gH}, a=-g\) and \(s=h_{1}\) [M1]\par \(0=2gHe^{2}-2gh_{1}\) [M1] [A1]\par \(\Rightarrow h_{1}=e^{2}H\) [A1]\par \textbf{b)} Let the height to which the ball rebounds after the second bounce be \(h_{2}\) [B1]\par Before the second bounce, the ball drops from a height \(h_{1}\) [M1] [B1]
So using the result from part a, \(h_{2}=e^{2}h_{1}\) [M1] [A1]

So \(h_{2}=e^{2}h_{1}=e^{2}(e^{2}H)=e^{4}H\) [A1]\par \textbf{c)} Let the total distance travelled by the ball be \(d\), then\par \(d=H+2h_{1}+2h_{2}+\dots\) [M1]\par \(=H+2e^{2}H+2e^{4}H+\dots\) [A1]\par \(=H+2e^{2}H(1+e^{2}+e^{4}+\dots)\) [M1]\par \(2e^{2}H(1+e^{2}+e^{4}+\dots)\) is an infinite geometric series with first term \(a=2e^{2}H\) and common ratio \(r=e^{2}\), so [B1]\par \(S_{\infty}=\frac{a}{1-r}=\frac{2e^{2}H}{1-e^{2}}\) [M1]\par Therefore\par \(d=H+2e^{2}H(1+e^{2}+e^{4}+\dots)=H+\frac{2e^{2}H}{1-e^{2}}\)\par \(=\frac{H(1-e^{2})+2e^{2}H}{1-e^{2}}=\frac{H+e^{2}H}{1-e^{2}}\)

transcription.tex: Question 9

A ball B lies on a smooth horizontal plane between two smooth, parallel, vertical walls \(W_{1}\) and \(W_{2}\) that are d m apart. B is initially halfway between the walls and is projected with velocity \(2\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) towards \(W_{2}\). The coefficient of restitution between B and \(W_{2}\) is \(e_{2}\) The ball then travels towards and strikes \(W_{1}\). The coefficient of restitution between B and \(W_{1}\) is \(e_{1}\) The ball then travels towards \(W_{2}\) again. Find, in terms of d, \(e_{1}\) and \(e_{2}\), the total time elapsed from the moment the ball is projected to the time when it strikes \(W_{2}\) for the second time. [9 marks]

From \(O \rightarrow W_{2},\)\par \(B\) travels at a speed of \(2\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) through a distance \(\frac{d}{2}\) m.\par So the time taken is \(\frac{\mathrm{distance}}{\mathrm{speed}}=\frac{\frac{d}{2}}{2}=\frac{d}{4}\) [M1] [A1]\par \(B\) then rebounds with speed \(2 e_{2}\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). [B1]\par From \(W_{2} \rightarrow W_{1},\)\par \(B\) travels at a speed of \(2 e_{2}\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) through a distance \(d\) m.
So the time taken is \(\frac{\mathrm{distance}}{\mathrm{speed}}=\frac{d}{2 e_{2}}\) [M1] [A1]

\(B\) then rebounds with speed \(2 e_{2} e_{1}\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). [B1]\par From \(W_{1} \rightarrow W_{2},\)\par \(B\) travels at a speed of \(2 e_{2} e_{1}\,\mathrm{~m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) through a distance \(d\) m.

So the time taken is \(\frac{\mathrm{distance}}{\mathrm{speed}}=\frac{d}{2 e_{2} e_{1}}\) [M1] [A1]\par Therefore, the total time taken is \(\frac{d}{4}+\frac{d}{2 e_{2}}+\frac{d}{2 e_{2} e_{1}}=\frac{d}{2} \left( \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{e_{1}}+\frac{1}{e_{1} e_{2}} \right)\) seconds. [A1]
